claim: In CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus, two types of AMPARs predominate: those that contain subunits GluA1 and GluA2 (GluA1/2), and those that contain GluA2 and GluA3 (GluA2/3).
source: In CA1 pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus two types of AMPARs predominate: those that contain subunits GluA1 and GluA2 (GluA1/2), and those that contain GluA2 and GluA3 (GluA2/3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Wenthold et al., 1996) and is consistent with established knowledge about AMPAR subunit composition in hippocampal neurons.

claim: GluA2/3s are in a low-conductance state under basal conditions.
source: Here we show in mice that GluA2/3s are in a low-conductance state under basal conditions, and although present at synapses they contribute little to synaptic currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-channel recordings and outside-out patch recordings showing low open-channel probability and conductance under basal conditions (Figure 2B).

claim: GluA2/3s are present at synapses under basal conditions.
source: Here we show in mice that GluA2/3s are in a low-conductance state under basal conditions, and although present at synapses they contribute little to synaptic currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experiments showing that SEP-GluA3 recovered to ~75% (Figure 4C), indicating that GluA2/3s are constitutively inserted into synapses.

claim: GluA2/3s contribute little to synaptic currents under basal conditions.
source: Here we show in mice that GluA2/3s are in a low-conductance state under basal conditions, and although present at synapses they contribute little to synaptic currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that extra-synaptic AMPAR currents recorded from GluA3-deficient neurons were similar to those from wild-type neurons (Figure 1A), and by prior studies (Lu et al., 2009; Meng et al., 2003).

claim: When intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels rise, GluA2/3 channels shift to a high-conductance state, leading to synaptic potentiation.
source: When intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels rise, GluA2/3 channels shift to a high-conductance state, leading to synaptic potentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased AMPAR currents in the presence of cAMP in GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 1A), increased open-channel probability and conductance (Figure 2B), and increased mEPSC frequency (Figure 3D).

claim: cAMP-driven synaptic potentiation requires the activation of both protein kinase A (PKA) and the GTPase Ras.
source: This cAMP-driven synaptic potentiation requires the activation of both protein kinase A (PKA) and the GTPase Ras, and is induced upon the activation of β-adrenergic receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that blocking both PKA and Ras prevented the forskolin-driven increase in mEPSC frequency in GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 6B).

claim: cAMP-driven synaptic potentiation is induced upon the activation of β-adrenergic receptors.
source: This cAMP-driven synaptic potentiation requires the activation of both protein kinase A (PKA) and the GTPase Ras, and is induced upon the activation of β-adrenergic receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that isoproterenol (a β-AR agonist) in the presence of IBMX increased mEPSC frequency in wild-type and GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 7), and that propranolol (a β-AR antagonist) blocked this effect (Figure 8B).

claim: Extra-synaptic AMPAR currents recorded from GluA3-deficient neurons were similar compared to those from wild-type neurons.
source: Extra-synaptic AMPAR currents recorded from GluA3-deficient neurons were similar compared to those from with wild-type neurons (t-test, p>0.9; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from outside-out patch recordings showing no significant difference in AMPAR currents between wild-type and GluA3-deficient neurons under basal conditions (Figure 1A).

claim: The absence of GluA3-containing AMPAR currents did not result in differences in the average number of functional AMPARs per patch, single channel conductance or open-channel probability.
source: A non-stationary noise analysis on these outside-out AMPAR currents showed that the absence of GluA3-containing AMPAR currents did not result in differences in the average number of functional AMPARs per patch, single channel conductance or open-channel probability (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from non-stationary noise analysis of outside-out recordings (Figure 1C,D).

claim: GluA1-deficient outside-out patches contained relatively few functional AMPAR channels.
source: Consistent with previous results (Andrásfalvy et al., 2003), GluA1-deficient outside-out patches contained relatively few functional AMPAR channels, and those that were present had a low single-channel conductance and open channel probability (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from non-stationary noise analysis (Figure 1C,D) and is consistent with prior literature (Andrásfalvy et al., 2003).

claim: GluA1-deficient AMPAR channels had a low single-channel conductance and open channel probability.
source: Consistent with previous results (Andrásfalvy et al., 2003), GluA1-deficient outside-out patches contained relatively few functional AMPAR channels, and those that were present had a low single-channel conductance and open channel probability (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from non-stationary noise analysis (Figure 1C,D) and is consistent with prior literature (Andrásfalvy et al., 2003).

claim: Currents were 83% smaller in the absence of GluA1.
source: As a result, currents were 83% smaller in the absence of GluA1 (t-test, p<0.0001; Figure 1A), indicating that under basal conditions the majority of extra-synaptic AMPAR currents are derived from GluA1-containing AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from outside-out patch recordings (Figure 1A).

claim: Under basal conditions the majority of extra-synaptic AMPAR currents are derived from GluA1-containing AMPARs.
source: As a result, currents were 83% smaller in the absence of GluA1 (t-test, p<0.0001; Figure 1A), indicating that under basal conditions the majority of extra-synaptic AMPAR currents are derived from GluA1-containing AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing 83% reduction in currents in GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 1A).

claim: In somatic membrane patches from wild-type neurons the amplitudes of the responses to AMPA puffs were 2-fold higher in the presence of cAMP.
source: In somatic membrane patches from wild-type neurons the amplitudes of the responses to AMPA puffs were 2-fold higher in the presence of cAMP (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from outside-out patch recordings with cAMP in the recording pipette (Figure 1A).

claim: In GluA3-deficient somatic patches cAMP failed to change AMPAR currents.
source: In GluA3-deficient somatic patches cAMP failed to change AMPAR currents Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from outside-out patch recordings showing no significant change in AMPAR currents in GluA3-deficient neurons in the presence of cAMP (Figure 1A).

claim: In GluA1-deficient CA1 patches AMPAR currents increased 4.5-fold in the presence of cAMP.
source: In GluA1-deficient CA1 patches AMPAR currents increased 4.5-fold in the presence of cAMP (Figure 1A), which occurred as a function of an increase in the estimated number of functional channels, channel conductance and open-channel probability (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from outside-out patch recordings (Figure 1A) and non-stationary noise analysis (Figure 1C,D).

claim: The increase in AMPAR currents in GluA1-deficient patches occurred as a function of an increase in the estimated number of functional channels, channel conductance and open-channel probability.
source: In GluA1-deficient CA1 patches AMPAR currents increased 4.5-fold in the presence of cAMP (Figure 1A), which occurred as a function of an increase in the estimated number of functional channels, channel conductance and open-channel probability (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from non-stationary noise analysis showing significant increases in all three parameters (Figure 1C,D).

claim: GluA3-containing AMPARs in GluA1-deficient patches activated by cAMP reached conductance levels comparable to those of GluA1-containing AMPARs in GluA3-deficient patches.
source: As a result, GluA3-containing AMPARs in GluA1-deficient patches activated by cAMP reached conductance levels comparable to those of GluA1-containing AMPARs in GluA3-deficient patches, the channel properties of which were not modified by cAMP (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from non-stationary noise analysis comparing conductance levels across genotypes (Figure 1C,D).

claim: cAMP selectively potentiated currents through extra-synaptic GluA3-containing AMPARs.
source: These experiments suggest that cAMP selectively potentiated currents through extra-synaptic GluA3-containing AMPARs, revealing a novel type of AMPAR plasticity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that cAMP increased currents in GluA1-deficient but not GluA3-deficient neurons (Figure 1A).

claim: Washing in both the adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin and PDE inhibitor IBMX rescued the cAMP-driven potentiation of AMPAR currents in GluA3-deficient neurons expressing SEP-GluA3.
source: Whereas SEP-GluA3 expression in GluA3-deficient neurons did not alter outside-out AMPAR currents, washing in both the adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin and PDE inhibitor IBMX rescued the cAMP-driven potentiation of AMPAR currents (Figure 1B), indicating that recombinant GluA3 responds similarly to a rise in cAMP as endogenous GluA3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from outside-out patch recordings in SEP-GluA3 infected GluA3-deficient neurons (Figure 1B).

claim: Recombinant GluA3 responds similarly to a rise in cAMP as endogenous GluA3.
source: Whereas SEP-GluA3 expression in GluA3-deficient neurons did not alter outside-out AMPAR currents, washing in both the adenylyl cyclase activator forskolin and PDE inhibitor IBMX rescued the cAMP-driven potentiation of AMPAR currents (Figure 1B), indicating that recombinant GluA3 responds similarly to a rise in cAMP as endogenous GluA3.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that recombinant SEP-GluA3 rescued the cAMP-driven potentiation (Figure 1B).

claim: The SEP fluorescence levels remained unchanged at the surface area of both dendrites and cell bodies upon the forskolin/IBMX wash-in.
source: However, the SEP fluorescence levels remained unchanged at the surface area of both dendrites and cell bodies upon the forskolin/IBMX wash-in (Figure 1E), suggesting that cAMP-driven GluA3-plasticity does not result from trafficking of GluA3-containing AMPARs from endocytic compartments to the cell surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon imaging of SEP-GluA3 fluorescence (Figure 1E).

claim: cAMP-driven GluA3-plasticity does not result from trafficking of GluA3-containing AMPARs from endocytic compartments to the cell surface.
source: However, the SEP fluorescence levels remained unchanged at the surface area of both dendrites and cell bodies upon the forskolin/IBMX wash-in (Figure 1E), suggesting that cAMP-driven GluA3-plasticity does not result from trafficking of GluA3-containing AMPARs from endocytic compartments to the cell surface.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no change in SEP fluorescence upon forskolin/IBMX treatment (Figure 1E).

claim: Single-channel currents of AMPARs recorded from GluA3-deficient neurons did not change in the presence of forskolin.
source: Single-channel currents of AMPARs recorded from GluA3-deficient neurons did not change in the presence of forskolin (Figure 2A), indicating that the channel properties of GluA1-containing AMPARs remained unchanged upon a rise in cAMP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-channel recordings under cell-attached configuration (Figure 2A).

claim: The channel properties of GluA1-containing AMPARs remained unchanged upon a rise in cAMP.
source: Single-channel currents of AMPARs recorded from GluA3-deficient neurons did not change in the presence of forskolin (Figure 2A), indicating that the channel properties of GluA1-containing AMPARs remained unchanged upon a rise in cAMP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no change in single-channel currents in GluA3-deficient neurons (Figure 2A).

claim: GluA2/3s at the surface of GluA1-deficient neurons had a low open-channel probability under basal conditions and remained largely stuck in open state 1.
source: In contrast, GluA2/3s at the surface of GluA1-deficient neurons had a low open-channel probability under basal conditions and remained largely stuck in open state 1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-channel recordings showing low open-channel probability and predominance of open state 1 (Figure 2B).

claim: In the presence of forskolin the open-channel probability was on average six-fold higher and GluA3-containing AMPARs more often reached open states 2 and 3.
source: In the presence of forskolin the open-channel probability was on average six-fold higher and GluA3-containing AMPARs more often reached open states 2 and 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-channel recordings in GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 2B).

claim: GluA3-containing AMPARs are largely electrically quiet under basal conditions, but become functional upon a rise in cAMP by increasing their capacity for glutamate-gated channel opening.
source: These experiments indicate that GluA3-containing AMPARs are largely electrically quiet under basal conditions, but become functional upon a rise in cAMP by increasing their capacity for glutamate-gated channel opening.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing low open-channel probability under basal conditions and increased open-channel probability upon forskolin treatment (Figure 2B).

claim: Forskolin incubation significantly increased AMPA/NMDA ratios evoked by stimulating Schaffer collateral inputs onto synapses of wild-type CA1 neurons.
source: Forskolin incubation significantly increased AMPA/NMDA ratios evoked by stimulating Schaffer collateral inputs onto synapses of wild-type CA1 neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recordings (Figure 3A).

claim: The potentiation effect of forskolin is predominantly postsynaptic.
source: Consistent with the notion that the potentiation effect of forskolin is predominantly postsynaptic (Sokolova et al., 2006), forskolin did not affect presynaptic glutamate release, since paired pulse ratios did not change (ANOVA: WT: p=0.8, KO: p=0.9; Figure 3B) and the quantal content of evoked glutamate release determined by a variance analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) did not increase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no change in paired pulse ratios (Figure 3B) and quantal content (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and is consistent with prior literature (Sokolova et al., 2006).

claim: Forskolin did not affect presynaptic glutamate release.
source: Consistent with the notion that the potentiation effect of forskolin is predominantly postsynaptic (Sokolova et al., 2006), forskolin did not affect presynaptic glutamate release, since paired pulse ratios did not change (ANOVA: WT: p=0.8, KO: p=0.9; Figure 3B) and the quantal content of evoked glutamate release determined by a variance analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) did not increase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no change in paired pulse ratios (Figure 3B) and quantal content (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: At Sc-CA1 synapses of GluA3-deficient neurons, forskolin did not change AMPA/NMDA ratios.
source: At Sc-CA1 synapses of GluA3-deficient neurons however, forskolin did not change AMPA/NMDA ratios (Figure 3A), indicating that a rise in cAMP triggers potentiation of postsynaptic GluA3-containing AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recordings in GluA3-deficient neurons (Figure 3A).

claim: A rise in cAMP triggers potentiation of postsynaptic GluA3-containing AMPARs.
source: At Sc-CA1 synapses of GluA3-deficient neurons however, forskolin did not change AMPA/NMDA ratios (Figure 3A), indicating that a rise in cAMP triggers potentiation of postsynaptic GluA3-containing AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that forskolin increased AMPA/NMDA ratios in wild-type but not GluA3-deficient neurons (Figure 3A).

claim: In miniature EPSC (mEPSC) recordings, the forskolin-driven postsynaptic potentiation was reflected as an increase in the frequency and amplitude of mEPSC events.
source: In miniature EPSC (mEPSC) recordings, the forskolin-driven postsynaptic potentiation was reflected as an increase in the frequency and amplitude of mEPSC events (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in wild-type neurons (Figure 3C).

claim: In GluA3-deficient neurons, forskolin did not significantly change the average mEPSC frequency or amplitude.
source: In GluA3-deficient neurons, forskolin did not significantly change the average mEPSC frequency or amplitude (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in GluA3-deficient neurons (Figure 3C).

claim: Re-introducing GluA3 in GluA3-deficient CA1 neurons by acute viral expression of GFP-GluA3 partially rescued the forskolin-driven synaptic potentiation.
source: Re-introducing GluA3 in GluA3-deficient CA1 neurons by acute viral expression of GFP-GluA3 and allowing it to be expressed for 24 hr partially rescued the forskolin-driven synaptic potentiation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in GFP-GluA3 infected GluA3-deficient neurons (Figure 3C).

claim: Neurons that are deficient in both GluA1 and GluA3 virtually lacked mEPSC events.
source: Neurons that are deficient in both GluA1 and GluA3 virtually lacked mEPSC events (Figure 3D), indicating that synaptic AMPAR currents recorded from GluA1-deficient CA1 neurons predominantly stem from GluA3-containing AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in GluA1/3 double deficient neurons (Figure 3D).

claim: Synaptic AMPAR currents recorded from GluA1-deficient CA1 neurons predominantly stem from GluA3-containing AMPARs.
source: Neurons that are deficient in both GluA1 and GluA3 virtually lacked mEPSC events (Figure 3D), indicating that synaptic AMPAR currents recorded from GluA1-deficient CA1 neurons predominantly stem from GluA3-containing AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that GluA1/3 double deficient neurons lacked mEPSC events (Figure 3D).

claim: Forskolin did elevate the mEPSC frequency in GluA1-deficient neurons.
source: Whereas these GluA1/GluA3 double deficient neurons were insensitive to forskolin, forskolin did elevate the mEPSC frequency in GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 3D).

claim: The synaptic AMPAR single-channel conductance was significantly increased by forskolin only when cells express GluA3.
source: To determine whether the cAMP-driven synaptic potentiation could be explained by increased single-channel conductance, we conducted peak-scaled non-stationary fluctuation analyses from mEPSCs. The synaptic AMPAR single-channel conductance was significantly increased by forskolin only when cells express GluA3 (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from non-stationary noise analysis of mEPSCs (Figure 3E,F).

claim: GluA1-deficient neurons displayed non-rectifying currents both in the absence and presence of forskolin.
source: GluA1-deficient neurons displayed non-rectifying currents both in the absence and presence of forskolin (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rectification index measurements (Figure 3H).

claim: When GFP-GluA3 was overexpressed in GluA3-deficient neurons, AMPAR currents remained non-rectifying in the presence of forskolin.
source: Also when GFP-GluA3 was overexpressed in GluA3-deficient neurons, AMPAR currents remained non-rectifying in the presence of forskolin (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rectification index measurements in GFP-GluA3 infected neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: GluA3-dependent plasticity at synapses predominantly stems from GluA2/3 heteromers.
source: These data indicate that GluA3-dependent plasticity at synapses predominantly stems from GluA2/3 heteromers.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing non-rectifying currents in GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 3H), which indicates the presence of GluA2-containing AMPARs.

claim: The SEP-GluA3 and SEP-GluA1 fluorescence intensity recovered at a similar pace irrespective of forskolin/IBMX being present.
source: After bleaching, the SEP-GluA3 and SEP-GluA1 fluorescence intensity recovered at a similar pace irrespective of forskolin/IBMX being present (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FRAP experiments (Figure 4B,C).

claim: GluA3 and GluA1 show a similar lateral mobility at the surface of spines, which did not change upon a rise in cAMP.
source: These data indicate that GluA3 and GluA1 show a similar lateral mobility at the surface of spines, which did not change upon a rise in cAMP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing similar FRAP recovery rates for SEP-GluA3 and SEP-GluA1 (Figure 4B,C).

claim: SEP-GluA1 fluorescence recovered to ~100%.
source: As shown previously (Makino and Malinow, 2009), SEP-GluA1 fluorescence recovered to ~100% (Figure 4B), indicating that GluA1-containing AMPARs are largely excluded from entry into synapses under basal conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FRAP experiments (Figure 4B) and is consistent with prior literature (Makino and Malinow, 2009).

claim: GluA1-containing AMPARs are largely excluded from entry into synapses under basal conditions.
source: As shown previously (Makino and Malinow, 2009), SEP-GluA1 fluorescence recovered to ~100% (Figure 4B), indicating that GluA1-containing AMPARs are largely excluded from entry into synapses under basal conditions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing ~100% FRAP recovery for SEP-GluA1 (Figure 4B) and is consistent with prior literature (Makino and Malinow, 2009).

claim: SEP-GluA3 recovered to ~75% both in the absence and presence of forskolin/IBMX.
source: SEP-GluA3 recovered to ~75% both in the absence and presence of forskolin/IBMX (Figure 4C), demonstrating that GluA2/3s are constitutively inserted into synapses independent of cAMP levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FRAP experiments (Figure 4C).

claim: GluA2/3s are constitutively inserted into synapses independent of cAMP levels.
source: SEP-GluA3 recovered to ~75% both in the absence and presence of forskolin/IBMX (Figure 4C), demonstrating that GluA2/3s are constitutively inserted into synapses independent of cAMP levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing ~75% FRAP recovery for SEP-GluA3 in both conditions (Figure 4C).

claim: Synaptic GluA3-plasticity is expressed by an increase in channel conductance of GluA3-containing AMPARs already present at synapses.
source: These experiments are consistent with the model that synaptic GluA3-plasticity is expressed by an increase in channel conductance of GluA3-containing AMPARs already present at synapses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no change in SEP-GluA3 levels at synapses upon forskolin treatment (Figure 4C) but increased single-channel conductance (Figure 3E,F).

claim: Adding the selective PKA activator N002 to the recording pipette significantly increased mEPSC frequency and amplitude in wild-type CA1 neurons.
source: In line with this, adding the selective PKA activator N002 to the recording pipette significantly increased mEPSC frequency and amplitude in wild-type CA1 neurons (Figure 5A), and not in GluA1-deficient CA1 neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings with N002 in the recording pipette (Figure 5A).

claim: N002 did not increase mEPSC frequency and amplitude in GluA1-deficient CA1 neurons.
source: In line with this, adding the selective PKA activator N002 to the recording pipette significantly increased mEPSC frequency and amplitude in wild-type CA1 neurons (Figure 5A), and not in GluA1-deficient CA1 neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings with N002 in GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 5B).

claim: PKA activation can trigger GluA1-dependent synaptic potentiation, but is not sufficient to promote GluA2/3-plasticity at synapses.
source: These data indicate that PKA activation can trigger GluA1-dependent synaptic potentiation, but is not sufficient to promote GluA2/3-plasticity at synapses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that N002 increased mEPSC frequency and amplitude in wild-type but not GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 5A,B).

claim: Pre-incubation of wild-type CA1 neurons with PKA-inhibitors PKI or KT 5720 failed to prevent the increase in mEPSC frequency.
source: Pre-incubation of wild-type CA1 neurons with PKA-inhibitors PKI (Figure 5C) or KT 5720 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) failed to prevent the increase in mEPSC frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings with PKI or KT 5720 preincubation (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: In GluA1-deficient CA1 neurons PKI also did not significantly block the forskolin-driven increase in mEPSC frequency.
source: In GluA1-deficient CA1 neurons PKI also did not significantly block the forskolin-driven increase in mEPSC frequency (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in GluA1-deficient neurons with PKI preincubation (Figure 5D).

claim: Epac/Rap1 signaling does not induce synaptic potentiation in CA1 neurons.
source: In line with previous studies (Gelinas et al., 2008; Ster et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2002), these data show that Epac/Rap1 signaling does not induce synaptic potentiation in CA1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect of Epac activation or inhibition (Figure 5E,F) and is consistent with prior literature (Gelinas et al., 2008; Ster et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2002).

claim: The FT-inhibitor Salirasib partially blocked the forskolin-mediated increase in mEPSC frequency.
source: The FT-inhibitor Salirasib partially blocked the forskolin-mediated increase in mEPSC frequency (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating that GluA2/3-plasticity involves a mediator that depends on FT activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings with Salirasib preincubation (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: GluA2/3-plasticity involves a mediator that depends on FT activity.
source: The FT-inhibitor Salirasib partially blocked the forskolin-mediated increase in mEPSC frequency (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating that GluA2/3-plasticity involves a mediator that depends on FT activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that Salirasib partially blocked the forskolin effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: The infusion of anti-Ras or control IgG did not affect basal synaptic transmission in both wild-type and GluA1-deficient neurons.
source: The infusion of anti-Ras or control IgG did not affect basal synaptic transmission in both wild-type and GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings with anti-Ras or control IgG in the recording pipette (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Upon the wash-in of forskolin, the mEPSC frequency gradually increased irrespective of the anti-Ras or control IgG being present.
source: Upon the wash-in of forskolin, the mEPSC frequency gradually increased irrespective of the anti-Ras or control IgG being present (Figure 6A,B, left), indicating that a blockade of Ras is not sufficient to prevent the cAMP-driven potentiation of GluA2/3 currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings with anti-Ras IgG in the recording pipette (Figure 6A,B).

claim: A blockade of Ras is not sufficient to prevent the cAMP-driven potentiation of GluA2/3 currents.
source: Upon the wash-in of forskolin, the mEPSC frequency gradually increased irrespective of the anti-Ras or control IgG being present (Figure 6A,B, left), indicating that a blockade of Ras is not sufficient to prevent the cAMP-driven potentiation of GluA2/3 currents.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that anti-Ras IgG alone did not prevent the forskolin effect (Figure 6A,B).

claim: When both PKA and Ras were blocked in wild-type CA1 neurons, the mEPSC frequency did not increase upon forskolin wash-in.
source: When both PKA and Ras were blocked in wild-type CA1 neurons, the mEPSC frequency did not increase upon forskolin wash-in, although the forskolin-mediated fold increase in mEPSC frequency was not significantly different between Ras and ctrl IgG (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings with both PKI and anti-Ras IgG (Figure 6A).

claim: In GluA1-deficient neurons, the blockade of both Ras and PKA did fully prevent the forskolin-driven fold increase in mEPSC frequency.
source: In GluA1-deficient neurons, in which the GluA2/3 currents are isolated, the blockade of both Ras and PKA did fully prevent the forskolin-driven fold increase in mEPSC frequency (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in GluA1-deficient neurons with both PKI and anti-Ras IgG (Figure 6B).

claim: The cAMP-driven signaling pathway that triggers activation of GluA2/3-plasticity requires the activation of both PKA and Ras.
source: These experiments indicate that the cAMP-driven signaling pathway that triggers activation of GluA2/3-plasticity requires the activation of both PKA and Ras.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that blocking both PKA and Ras prevented the forskolin effect in GluA1-deficient neurons (Figure 6B).

claim: Isoproterenol in the presence of IBMX increased mEPSC frequency in CA1 neurons of both wild-type and GluA1-deficient mice.
source: When these slices were incubated with isoproterenol we observed an increased frequency, but not amplitude, of mEPSC events in CA1 neurons of both wild-type and GluA1-deficient mice, provided that PDE activity was inhibited with IBMX (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in acute brain slices with isoproterenol and IBMX (Figure 7).

claim: Isoproterenol did not trigger synaptic potentiation in CA1 neurons of GluA3-deficient brain slices.
source: Isoproterenol did not trigger synaptic potentiation in CA1 neurons of GluA3-deficient brain slices (Figure 7), indicating that β-AR activation can evoke GluA3-dependent plasticity upon a robust increase in cAMP levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in GluA3-deficient acute brain slices (Figure 7).

claim: β-AR activation can evoke GluA3-dependent plasticity upon a robust increase in cAMP levels.
source: Isoproterenol did not trigger synaptic potentiation in CA1 neurons of GluA3-deficient brain slices (Figure 7), indicating that β-AR activation can evoke GluA3-dependent plasticity upon a robust increase in cAMP levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that isoproterenol/IBMX increased mEPSC frequency in wild-type and GluA1-deficient but not GluA3-deficient neurons (Figure 7).

claim: E-injection decreased the locomotion of wild-type, GluA3-deficient and GluA1-deficient mice.
source: When mice were placed in a novel environment 10 min after E-injection, wild-type, GluA3-deficient and GluA1-deficient mice showed decreased locomotion (Figure 8A), suggesting that LC-activity is intact in GluA3- and GluA1-deficient mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from locomotion measurements after E-injection (Figure 8A).

claim: LC-activity is intact in GluA3- and GluA1-deficient mice.
source: When mice were placed in a novel environment 10 min after E-injection, wild-type, GluA3-deficient and GluA1-deficient mice showed decreased locomotion (Figure 8A), suggesting that LC-activity is intact in GluA3- and GluA1-deficient mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that E-injection decreased locomotion in all genotypes (Figure 8A).

claim: In brain slices prepared 10 min after E-injection, a significant increase in mEPSC frequency was observed in CA1 neurons of wild-type and GluA1-deficient mice compared with saline-injected littermates.
source: In brain slices prepared 10 min after E-injection we observed a significant increase in mEPSC frequency in CA1 neurons of wild-type and GluA1-deficient mice compared with saline-injected littermates (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in brain slices prepared after E-injection (Figure 8B).

claim: No increase in mEPSC frequency was detected when GluA1-deficient mice were injected with β-AR antagonist propranolol 20 min prior to E-injection.
source: No increase in mEPSC frequency was detected when GluA1-deficient mice were injected with β-AR antagonist propranolol 20 min prior to E-injection (Figure 8B), indicating that potentiation of GluA2/3-currents depended on β-AR activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in brain slices prepared after E-injection with propranolol pretreatment (Figure 8B).

claim: Potentiation of GluA2/3-currents depended on β-AR activation.
source: No increase in mEPSC frequency was detected when GluA1-deficient mice were injected with β-AR antagonist propranolol 20 min prior to E-injection (Figure 8B), indicating that potentiation of GluA2/3-currents depended on β-AR activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that propranolol blocked the E-injection effect (Figure 8B).

claim: In slices isolated from E-injected GluA3-deficient mice, no increase in mEPSC events was detected.
source: In slices isolated from E-injected GluA3-deficient mice we failed to detect an increase in mEPSC events (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in GluA3-deficient brain slices prepared after E-injection (Figure 8B).

claim: The synaptic effect of E-injection was evident in slices prepared from mice injected with control GFP-virus.
source: Whereas the synaptic effect of E-injection was evident in slices prepared from mice injected with control GFP-virus, it was significantly reduced in neurons where GluA3 expression had been stopped out by Cre-GFP (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in GFP-infected neurons after E-injection (Figure 8C).

claim: The synaptic effect of E-injection was significantly reduced in neurons where GluA3 expression had been stopped out by Cre-GFP.
source: Whereas the synaptic effect of E-injection was evident in slices prepared from mice injected with control GFP-virus, it was significantly reduced in neurons where GluA3 expression had been stopped out by Cre-GFP (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mEPSC recordings in Cre-GFP infected neurons after E-injection (Figure 8C).

claim: NE-release induces potentiation of GluA2/3-currents at CA1 pyramidal synapses in the hippocampus.
source: These data indicate that NE-release induces potentiation of GluA2/3-currents at CA1 pyramidal synapses in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that E-injection increased mEPSC frequency in a GluA3-dependent manner (Figure 8B,C).

claim: The total protein levels of GluA3 in the hippocampus are substantial.
source: However, the total protein levels of GluA3 in the hippocampus were shown to be substantial (Schwenk et al., 2014), and it was estimated that the AMPAR population in CA1 dendrites is composed of equivalent amounts of GluA1/2s and GluA2/3s (Kessels et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Schwenk et al., 2014).

claim: The AMPAR population in CA1 dendrites is composed of equivalent amounts of GluA1/2s and GluA2/3s.
source: However, the total protein levels of GluA3 in the hippocampus were shown to be substantial (Schwenk et al., 2014), and it was estimated that the AMPAR population in CA1 dendrites is composed of equivalent amounts of GluA1/2s and GluA2/3s (Kessels et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Kessels et al., 2009).

claim: GluA3-containing AMPARs are present at synapses and on the cell surface; however, they are electrically quiet under basal conditions.
source: We here unify these seemingly contradictory findings by showing that GluA3-containing AMPARs are present at synapses and on the cell surface; however, they are electrically quiet under basal conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that GluA3-containing AMPARs are present at synapses (Figure 4C) but contribute little to currents under basal conditions (Figure 1A, Figure 2B).

claim: The cAMP-driven activation of GluA2/3s at the surface of cell bodies mirrors GluA2/3-plasticity at synapses: both increased approximately two-fold in currents upon a rise in cAMP.
source: The cAMP-driven activation of GluA2/3s at the surface of cell bodies mirrors GluA2/3-plasticity at synapses: both increased approximately two-fold in currents upon a rise in cAMP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing similar fold increases in currents at both extrasynaptic (Figure 1A) and synaptic (Figure 3A) sites.

claim: Approximately half of the synaptic and extrasynaptic AMPAR population consists of GluA2/3s.
source: These results imply that similar to its total levels at CA1 dendrites (Kessels et al., 2009) approximately half of the synaptic and extrasynaptic AMPAR population consists of GluA2/3s.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that cAMP increased currents approximately two-fold (Figure 1A, Figure 3A) and is consistent with prior literature (Kessels et al., 2009).

claim: When recombinant GluA3 was acutely expressed in GluA3-deficient CA1 neurons of organotypic slices, the newly formed GluA3-containing AMPARs were inserted onto to the surface and into synapses without a change in synaptic or extrasynaptic AMPAR currents.
source: When recombinant GluA3 was acutely expressed in GluA3-deficient CA1 neurons of organotypic slices, the newly formed GluA3-containing AMPARs were inserted onto to the surface and into synapses without a change in synaptic or extrasynaptic AMPAR currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that SEP-GluA3 expression did not alter outside-out AMPAR currents (Figure 1B) but was present at synapses (Figure 4C).

claim: Upon a rise in cAMP, recombinant GluA3-containing AMPARs showed increased currents at both synaptic and extrasynaptic sites without a change in GluA3 levels at synapses or at the cell surface.
source: However, upon a rise in cAMP they showed increased currents at both synaptic and extrasynaptic sites without a change in GluA3 levels at synapses or at the cell surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased currents upon forskolin/IBMX (Figure 1B, Figure 3C) without changes in SEP-GluA3 fluorescence (Figure 1E, Figure 4C).

claim: GluA3-containing AMPARs constitutively traffic into synapses in an inactive state and only contribute to synaptic currents after cAMP levels have risen.
source: Our results therefore indicate that GluA3-containing AMPARs constitutively traffic into synapses in an inactive state and only contribute to synaptic currents after cAMP levels have risen.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that GluA3-containing AMPARs are present at synapses (Figure 4C) but contribute little to currents under basal conditions (Figure 1A, Figure 2B), and that currents increase upon cAMP elevation (Figure 1A, Figure 3C).

claim: GluA1-containing AMPARs are largely kept out of the synapse under basal conditions and require LTP-like activity to traffic into synapses.
source: In contrast, GluA1-containing AMPARs are largely kept out of the synapse under basal conditions and require LTP-like activity to traffic into synapses (Kessels et al., 2009; Makino and Malinow, 2009; Shi et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Kessels et al., 2009; Makino and Malinow, 2009; Shi et al., 2001) and is consistent with the FRAP data showing ~100% recovery for SEP-GluA1 (Figure 4B).

claim: LTP can be expressed by the insertion of both GluA1-containing and GluA1-lacking AMPARs into synapses.
source: A recent study showed that LTP can be expressed by the insertion of both GluA1-containing and GluA1-lacking AMPARs into synapses (Granger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Granger et al., 2013).

claim: The finding that GluA2/3s are electrically dormant under basal conditions may explain why LTP is not visible in GluA1-deficient hippocampal slices.
source: Although this study did not show whether this is also the case for GluA2/3s, our finding that GluA2/3s are electrically dormant under basal conditions may explain why LTP is not visible in GluA1-deficient hippocampal slices (Granger et al., 2013; Humeau et al., 2007; Zamanillo et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that GluA2/3s are electrically dormant under basal conditions (Figure 2B) and is consistent with prior literature showing impaired LTP in GluA1-deficient slices (Granger et al., 2013; Humeau et al., 2007; Zamanillo et al., 1999).

claim: A slowly arising LTP can be seen in GluA1-deficient slices when a theta-burst stimulation is paired with a postsynaptic depolarization.
source: A previous study showed that a slowly arising LTP can be seen in GluA1-deficient slices when a theta-burst stimulation is paired with a postsynaptic depolarization (Frey et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Frey et al., 2009).

claim: Upon theta-burst stimulation paired with postsynaptic depolarization, a gradual increase in cAMP levels may have activated GluA2/3-plasticity.
source: We speculate that upon this stimulation protocol a gradual increase in cAMP levels may have activated GluA2/3-plasticity.
evidence: This claim is speculative and is based on the inference that the stimulation protocol may have increased cAMP levels.

claim: GluA1/2s and GluA2/3s are differentially distributed at CA1 synapses.
source: An increase in mEPSC frequency rather than mEPSC amplitude upon the activation of GluA2/3-plasticity may be further explained by the findings that GluA1/2s and GluA2/3s are differentially distributed at CA1 synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Jacob and Weinberg, 2015; Shinohara and Hirase, 2009).

claim: GluA3 is uniformly distributed within synapses.
source: Whereas GluA3 is uniformly distributed within synapses, GluA1 tends to be more concentrated towards their edges (Jacob and Weinberg, 2015) and large CA1 synapses are particularly enriched in GluA1 (Shinohara and Hirase, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Jacob and Weinberg, 2015).

claim: GluA1 tends to be more concentrated towards the edges of synapses.
source: Whereas GluA3 is uniformly distributed within synapses, GluA1 tends to be more concentrated towards their edges (Jacob and Weinberg, 2015) and large CA1 synapses are particularly enriched in GluA1 (Shinohara and Hirase, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Jacob and Weinberg, 2015).

claim: Large CA1 synapses are particularly enriched in GluA1.
source: Whereas GluA3 is uniformly distributed within synapses, GluA1 tends to be more concentrated towards their edges (Jacob and Weinberg, 2015) and large CA1 synapses are particularly enriched in GluA1 (Shinohara and Hirase, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Shinohara and Hirase, 2009).

claim: GluA3-containing AMPARs are present in most brain regions, including the cortex, amygdala, striatum, thalamus, brain stem, olfactory bulb, nucleus accumbens and cerebellum.
source: Besides the hippocampus, GluA3-containing AMPARs are present in most other brain regions, including the cortex, amygdala, striatum, thalamus, brain stem, olfactory bulb, nucleus accumbens and cerebellum (Breese et al., 1996; Reimers et al., 2011; Schwenk et al., 2014), suggesting that GluA2/3-plasticity may be operative throughout the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Breese et al., 1996; Reimers et al., 2011; Schwenk et al., 2014).

claim: GluA2/3-plasticity may be operative throughout the brain.
source: Besides the hippocampus, GluA3-containing AMPARs are present in most other brain regions, including the cortex, amygdala, striatum, thalamus, brain stem, olfactory bulb, nucleus accumbens and cerebellum (Breese et al., 1996; Reimers et al., 2011; Schwenk et al., 2014), suggesting that GluA2/3-plasticity may be operative throughout the brain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the widespread distribution of GluA3-containing AMPARs in the brain.

claim: GluA3-deficient mice show increased social and aggressive behavior.
source: For instance, GluA3-deficient mice show increased social and aggressive behavior (Adamczyk et al., 2012), a reduced alcohol-seeking behavior (Sanchis-Segura et al., 2006), impaired auditory processing (García-Hernández et al., 2017), and altered electroencephalographic patterns in the cortex during sleep (Steenland et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Adamczyk et al., 2012).

claim: GluA3-deficient mice show a reduced alcohol-seeking behavior.
source: For instance, GluA3-deficient mice show increased social and aggressive behavior (Adamczyk et al., 2012), a reduced alcohol-seeking behavior (Sanchis-Segura et al., 2006), impaired auditory processing (García-Hernández et al., 2017), and altered electroencephalographic patterns in the cortex during sleep (Steenland et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Sanchis-Segura et al., 2006).

claim: GluA3-deficient mice show impaired auditory processing.
source: For instance, GluA3-deficient mice show increased social and aggressive behavior (Adamczyk et al., 2012), a reduced alcohol-seeking behavior (Sanchis-Segura et al., 2006), impaired auditory processing (García-Hernández et al., 2017), and altered electroencephalographic patterns in the cortex during sleep (Steenland et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (García-Hernández et al., 2017).

claim: GluA3-deficient mice show altered electroencephalographic patterns in the cortex during sleep.
source: For instance, GluA3-deficient mice show increased social and aggressive behavior (Adamczyk et al., 2012), a reduced alcohol-seeking behavior (Sanchis-Segura et al., 2006), impaired auditory processing (García-Hernández et al., 2017), and altered electroencephalographic patterns in the cortex during sleep (Steenland et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Steenland et al., 2008).

claim: Motor learning and the expression of LTP in Purkinje cells did not require GluA1, but critically depended on GluA3.
source: We found that the AMPAR-subunit specific rules for synaptic plasticity in PCs were reversed compared with CA1 neurons: motor learning and the expression of LTP did not require GluA1, but critically depended on GluA3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).

claim: GluA3-dependent plasticity in Purkinje cells is mediated by Epac/Rap1.
source: Similarly as at CA1 synapses, synaptic potentiation was accomplished by the activation of GluA3-channel function upon a rise in cAMP. An interesting difference is that GluA3-dependent plasticity in PCs is mediated by Epac/Rap1 (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).

claim: The activation of β-ARs at CA1 neurons of the hippocampus can stimulate two independent forms of AMPAR plasticity in parallel.
source: The activation of β-ARs at CA1 neurons of the hippocampus can stimulate two independent forms of AMPAR plasticity in parallel.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that β-AR activation can trigger both GluA1-dependent (Man et al., 2007) and GluA3-dependent (Figure 7, Figure 8) plasticity.

claim: PKA phosphorylation of GluA1-containing AMPARs facilitates their trafficking to synapses.
source: First, PKA phosphorylation of GluA1-containing AMPARs facilitates their trafficking to synapses (Man et al., 2007), thereby facilitating memory formation (Hu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Man et al., 2007).

claim: PKA phosphorylation of GluA1-containing AMPARs facilitates memory formation.
source: First, PKA phosphorylation of GluA1-containing AMPARs facilitates their trafficking to synapses (Man et al., 2007), thereby facilitating memory formation (Hu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Hu et al., 2007).

claim: GluA2/3s at synapses increase their currents upon β-AR activation.
source: We identified a second cAMP-dependent form of AMPAR plasticity. Our data show that GluA2/3s at synapses increase their currents upon β-AR activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that β-AR activation increased mEPSC frequency in a GluA3-dependent manner (Figure 7, Figure 8).
